title: What the Eye Sends the Brain

scenes.visual: Silent title card, 3.0 seconds: "What the Eye Sends the Brain".

scenes.tts: Every signal the brain gets from the eye leaves through ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve. But the optic nerve is not a camera cable. A mouse has more than forty types of ganglion cell, and each type sends the brain a different feature of the scene. Some signal local differences in brightness. Others detect a small moving object, or motion in one direction. Circuits inside the retina build each feature before any spike leaves the eye.

scenes.visual: A scene of a field and sky enters an eye; instead of one cable, many coloured strands leave through the optic nerve, each carrying a small icon (contrast patch, small moving dot, upward arrow).

scenes.tts: Take the W three cell. It pools excitation from the O N and O F F pathways, so a local change of either sign excites it. Much of that excitation arrives through an excitatory amacrine cell. When the distant surround moves too, the circuit suppresses that excitation and inhibits the cell. So W three fires for a small object moving against a still background, and falls quiet when the whole scene moves.
scenes.narration: Take the W3 cell. It pools excitation from the ON and OFF pathways, so a local change of either sign excites it. Much of that excitation arrives through an excitatory amacrine cell. When the distant surround moves too, the circuit suppresses that excitation and inhibits the cell. So W3 fires for a small object moving against a still background, and falls quiet when the whole scene moves.

scenes.visual: Split panel: left, a small dot moves over a still background and a W3 spike train fills with ticks; right, the whole background slides and the spike train goes flat while wide amacrine processes in the surround light up.

scenes.tts: A second channel is the J A M B cell, an O F F cell with a lopsided dendritic arbor. These asymmetric cells preferred one direction of motion, from the cell body toward the dendrites. Other channels report contrast, colour, or light level. Information that no channel carries is gone before the brain has a chance.

scenes.visual: An asymmetric arbor points one way on the retina and a stimulus bar sweeps from soma to dendrite tips; then a few strands leave the eye and one gap is marked empty.

scenes.tts: How do we know a channel is a real type? Three kinds of evidence can define one: a shared light response, dendritic shape, and gene expression profile. A cluster is not yet a type. A type is supported when these agree, and when its cells are spaced in a regular mosaic, though some real types are only weakly regular.

scenes.visual: Response, shape and expression chips join around a gold type ring; evenly spaced cell bodies with overlapping dendrites; a teal cluster blob outside the ring is labelled "not yet a type".

scenes.tts: Each method counts by its own evidence. Imaging grouped cells by light response and found at least thirty two types. Sequencing found forty six. Recording from single cells found forty two. Electron microscopy supported at least thirty five. These are not rival answers. Each reflects a method and a resolution, and the authors read them as converging on about forty five.
scenes.narration: Each method counts by its own evidence. Imaging grouped cells by light response and found at least 32 types. Sequencing found 46. Recording from single cells found 42. Electron microscopy supported at least 35. These are not rival answers. Each reflects a method and a resolution, and the authors read them as converging on about 45.

scenes.visual: Four count cards appear, each tagged with its method icon (microscope, droplet, pipette, electron beam); the cards slide together toward a single band marked about 45.

scenes.tts: Mouse is not macaque. The primate fovea is packed with midget ganglion cells, each fed through a bipolar cell by a single cone, and that private line supports sharp vision. In the macaque fovea, midget clusters made up about eighty five percent of sampled ganglion cells. Shared ancestry with mouse cells does not mean a shared size, frequency, or job.

In the macaque fovea, midget clusters made up about 85% of sampled ganglion cells. Shared ancestry with mouse cells does not mean a shared size, frequency, or job.

scenes.visual: A foveal cone array with one-to-one lines to midget cells; a pie of sampled foveal cells, mostly midget; a sparse mouse alpha cell beside a dense primate midget mosaic.

scenes.tts: So the eye does not send the brain a picture. It sends dozens of filtered versions of the scene, side by side, and the brain can only work with what those channels deliver.
